category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A financial services organization has built a custom machine learning (ML) model designed for real-time fraud detection. The model, which is hosted on the company’s on-premises infrastructure, is less than 5 GB in size and processes up to 50 concurrent requests simultaneously. The company is exploring AWS services to migrate its model to the cloud while minimizing infrastructure management. The development team is familiar with Amazon Rekognition for image-based analysis and Amazon Textract for document analysis, and is now looking for the best service to deploy the fraud detection model. Which of the following will meet the given requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy the custom fraud detection model in Amazon SageMaker Neo to optimize the model, then host the optimized model on a SageMaker real‑time endpoint.
Create a model configuration within Amazon SageMaker AI, then deploy the custom fraud detection model on a serverless SageMaker endpoint.
Create a model configuration within Amazon SageMaker AI, then deploy the custom fraud detection model on an asynchronous SageMaker endpoint.
options.rationale: because asynchronous endpoints are primarily designed for batch or long-running inference tasks, not real-time use cases. Fraud detection requires immediate responses, so this option would introduce unacceptable latency.

options.text: Deploy the fraud detection model on a highly available Amazon EC2 instance in an auto-scaling group. Configure an application load balancer to route the incoming requests to the EC2 instance.
options.rationale: because it involves significant infrastructure management, provisioning, scaling, patching, and configuring load balancing. This goes against the goal of minimizing operational overhead.

correct_text: Create a model configuration within Amazon SageMaker AI, then deploy the custom fraud detection model on a serverless SageMaker endpoint.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A travel booking company runs an AI-powered trip recommendation platform on Amazon EC2 instances. The application makes API calls to Amazon Bedrock foundation models to analyze traveler preferences, destination data, and booking history before generating personalized itinerary suggestions. The company occasionally sees lower-quality recommendations, unexpected increases in token consumption, and slower model responses for certain trip types and customer segments. The operations team needs a centralized observability solution that can correlate application health with model behavior, detect unusual deviations from established performance patterns, and analyze logs to identify recurring causes of degraded recommendations. Which approach will provide the required observability with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging and send the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Create metric filters for token usage and response latency, and configure static CloudWatch alarms when predefined thresholds are exceeded.
options.rationale: because static alarms typically compare metrics against fixed thresholds rather than adapt to established patterns in historical behavior. This approach also does not create a custom recommendation-quality metric segmented by request type and user group, limiting the company’s ability to correlate degraded output quality with specific workload characteristics. CloudWatch anomaly detection is better aligned with the requirement to identify deviations from normal performance baselines.

options.text: Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the EC2 instances to collect CPU, memory, disk, and application logs. Create CloudWatch dashboards for the infrastructure metrics and manually review Bedrock API latency when recommendation quality declines.
options.rationale: because this configuration would primarily provide infrastructure and host-level visibility. CPU, memory, and disk metrics do not directly measure recommendation quality or token consumption, and manual investigation does not satisfy the requirement to automatically detect unusual model behavior and correlate it with application performance.

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray tracing for the application and Bedrock API calls. Use trace data to identify slow requests, publish average latency metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, and configure alarms for requests that exceed fixed response-time thresholds.
options.rationale: because tracing would simply focus on request paths and latency rather than provide the multidimensional business and model-quality metrics required in the scenario. It also relies on fixed latency thresholds and does not provide the adaptive baseline monitoring or log-pattern analysis needed to detect broader recommendation-quality and token-usage anomalies.

options.text: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights to monitor the application resources. Publish custom metrics for recommendation quality, token consumption, and response latency using the embedded metric format, segmented by request type and user group. Apply CloudWatch anomaly detection to the model metrics and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to identify recurring performance patterns.

correct_text: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights to monitor the application resources. Publish custom metrics for recommendation quality, token consumption, and response latency using the embedded metric format, segmented by request type and user group. Apply CloudWatch anomaly detection to the model metrics and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to identify recurring performance patterns.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A global media company is designing a generative AI platform to automate the creation of video scripts and personalized marketing content. The platform relies on Amazon SageMaker AI to fine-tune a proprietary large language model (LLM) using terabytes of internal marketing and audience data. Meanwhile, Amazon Comprehend is used to perform real-time sentiment analysis and extract entity information from customer feedback. This enables the LLM to generate content that is contextually relevant and aligned with audience sentiment. The training dataset is extensive, and the model contains hundreds of billions of parameters, requiring highly optimized and scalable infrastructure to minimize training time and cost. Which Amazon EC2 instance type is the most appropriate choice for the fine-tuning workload?

options.text: Deploy GPU-based P series EC2 instances to train the LLM and serve it via SageMaker AI endpoints.
options.rationale: . P-series instances are primarily designed for standard ML training tasks and general GPU acceleration. They can handle moderate-sized models efficiently, but they are simply not optimized for extremely large LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters. Using P-series for this workload would typically result in longer training times and higher costs due to insufficient GPU memory and interconnect bandwidth for distributed training at scale.

options.text: Select purpose-built Trn series EC2 instances that are optimised for high-performance training of large language models (LLMs).
Use general-purpose M-series EC2 instances with SageMaker AI for distributed training.
options.rationale: . M-series instances are only intended for general-purpose computing and lightweight ML workloads. They lack GPU acceleration and the specialized memory and interconnect performance required for large-scale LLM fine-tuning. Using M-series would typically lead to significant training bottlenecks and would be impractical for efficiently processing terabytes of data.

options.text: Leverage accelerated‑computing G series EC2 instances to deploy a smaller version of the generative model after pre‑processing via Comprehend.
options.rationale: . G-series instances are primarily designed for graphics-intensive workloads, such as rendering and visualization, and are not optimized for high-performance ML training. While they can run smaller inference tasks, they are insufficient for training extremely large LLMs, as their architecture cannot handle the memory and computational requirements of hundreds-of-billion-parameter models.

correct_text: Select purpose-built Trn series EC2 instances that are optimised for high-performance training of large language models (LLMs).

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A financial analytics firm uses Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Comprehend to detect potential fraud patterns across millions of real-time financial transactions. Comprehend extracts critical text features such as transaction context, merchant type, and sentiment from unstructured financial notes, while SageMaker AI consumes this enriched dataset to train and deploy a fraud detection model that classifies transactions as legitimate or suspicious. A newly optimized model version has recently been retrained in SageMaker AI using improved training features and hyperparameters. The data science team must evaluate the new model’s prediction accuracy and latency in production without impacting the throughput of the currently deployed model. Additionally, the deployment process must introduce minimal operational overhead and must not require any changes to the way the inference endpoint is invoked by clients. Which of the following options will satisfy the given requirements?

options.text: Register the new model version in SageMaker Model Registry and configure an event trigger in AWS Lambda to automatically swap the endpoint to the new model after initial validation.
options.rationale: because it primarily replaces the existing model entirely, preventing side-by-side evaluation. This approach risks production stability and introduces unnecessary complexity with Lambda automation and registry workflows.

options.text: Deploy both models in separate SageMaker endpoints and use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to compare their results in post-processing.
options.rationale: because it typically requires managing multiple endpoints and manually routing traffic, which increases operational overhead. It also violates the requirement that clients should not have to change how they invoke the inference endpoint.

options.text: Configure an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that splits traffic between the current and the new SageMaker endpoints for A/B testing.
options.rationale: because it introduces additional infrastructure and requires clients to invoke a new API Gateway endpoint instead of the existing SageMaker endpoint. This contradicts the requirement of maintaining the same client invocation method.

options.text: Modify the existing SageMaker AI endpoint configuration by adding the new model as a ProductionVariant through the ProductionVariant API, and set a small InitialVariantWeight compared to the existing model’s ProductionVariant VariantWeight to control the percentage of traffic routed to it.

correct_text: Modify the existing SageMaker AI endpoint configuration by adding the new model as a ProductionVariant through the ProductionVariant API, and set a small InitialVariantWeight compared to the existing model’s ProductionVariant VariantWeight to control the percentage of traffic routed to it.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A financial analytics company is building a customer-facing chatbot that uses a large language model (LLM) to answer domain-specific questions about investment products and compliance policies. The company has thousands of PDF documents stored in an Amazon S3 bucket that contain detailed policy explanations and financial regulations. The AI engineering team wants the chatbot to retrieve precise answers from these documents instead of relying solely on the LLM’s pre-trained knowledge. The goal is to implement a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach to ground the model’s responses with proprietary data. The team is evaluating whether to use Amazon Kendra or Amazon Bedrock to manage this retrieval pipeline efficiently while maintaining scalability and minimal infrastructure overhead. Which solution provides the most effective and AWS-managed way to integrate proprietary document retrieval with an LLM for this RAG-based chatbot?

options.text: Deploy Kendra as an independent search engine to index the documents in the S3 bucket. Configure the LLM to query Kendra’s search results directly for every user request.
options.rationale: . While Amazon Kendra can index and semantically search the S3 documents, it is only a retrieval service. It does not natively perform retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) integration with a large language model. Building a custom connection between Kendra and an LLM would require manual orchestration, data formatting, and prompt engineering. This approach would simply increase operational complexity and reduce the benefits of a fully managed, scalable solution like Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

options.text: Fine-tune the LLM in Bedrock on the text extracted from the S3 bucket so that the model permanently learns the organization’s policies and eliminates the need for document retrieval.
options.rationale: . Fine-tuning is typically used to adjust a model’s tone, structure, or task-specific behavior, not to embed continuously changing enterprise knowledge. Fine-tuning permanently modifies model parameters and would require repeated retraining whenever new policies or regulations are added. This method would be costly, time-consuming, and not suitable for regulatory data that must remain up-to-date. In contrast, RAG allows models to dynamically reference the latest proprietary documents without altering the base model, which is far more efficient and maintainable.

options.text: Configure a knowledge base in Bedrock. Add the S3 bucket as the connected data source, and utilize the Bedrock API to perform RAG queries that dynamically combine document retrieval with LLM generation.
Use Kendra to extract document embeddings then store it manually in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Query the embeddings from a custom inference endpoint for every RAG request.
options.rationale: . Amazon Kendra does not directly export document embeddings for custom use, and storing such data in DynamoDB adds unnecessary overhead. Developers would have to handle embedding generation, vector storage, and nearest-neighbor search logic independently. This solution would simply replicate capabilities already offered natively through Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which automate the ingestion, embedding, retrieval, and integration of proprietary content into model responses.

correct_text: Configure a knowledge base in Bedrock. Add the S3 bucket as the connected data source, and utilize the Bedrock API to perform RAG queries that dynamically combine document retrieval with LLM generation.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: An enterprise is modernizing its internal operations by building a generative AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock Agents. Employees will use the assistant to handle complex customer service and operational requests, such as: Retrieving customer account and transaction data from internal systems. Applying regulatory and compliance checks before responding. Generating customer-friendly explanations using a foundation model. Triggering downstream actions such as opening support tickets, sending notifications, or updating CRM records. Each of these steps requires different permissions, tools, APIs, and reasoning logic. The goal is to design a modular, scalable, and easy to evolve as business rules and compliance requirements change. Minimizing custom orchestration code outside of Bedrock is also important. Which solution design should the enterprise use to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a single Bedrock agent with one large system prompt and a single action group that sequentially handles intent detection, data retrieval, compliance checks, and workflow execution.
options.rationale: because. Combining intent detection, data retrieval, compliance evaluation, workflow execution, and response generation into one agent makes the logic hard to maintain, update, or secure. A single agent cannot easily isolate domain-specific responsibilities, and it primarily increases the risk of errors in multi-step workflows. While technically possible, this approach just does not scale well for enterprise scenarios with multiple specialized requirements.

options.text: Create multiple foundation models hosted in Bedrock and implement custom routing logic in the application layer to manually pass user requests between models, using multi-agent coordination tracking to monitor task handoffs.
options.rationale: because building custom routing logic outside of Bedrock directly contradicts the requirement of minimizing custom orchestration code. Managing multiple foundation models through a custom application layer introduces significant operational overhead and complexity. Additionally, multi-agent coordination tracking does not compensate for the lack of native Bedrock orchestration, as it only monitors task handoffs but does not provide the modular, scalable agent collaboration that the requirements demand.

options.text: Create a Bedrock knowledge base and rely primarily on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to answer all user requests.
options.rationale: because retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) only retrieves information from a knowledge base. It just cannot perform multi-step reasoning, call APIs, or trigger downstream actions, which are critical requirements in this scenario. RAG is primarily designed to answer questions based on stored documents, and relying solely on it does not provide the orchestration and task specialization needed for complex enterprise workflows involving multiple steps and tools.

options.text: Create multi-agent collaboration by defining multiple Bedrock agents, each specializing in a specific responsibility and collaborating with other agents to complete the end-to-end request.

correct_text: Create multi-agent collaboration by defining multiple Bedrock agents, each specializing in a specific responsibility and collaborating with other agents to complete the end-to-end request.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A company is modernizing its customer support assistant for product troubleshooting, delivery updates, and return requests. The assistant processes thousands of daily queries, retrieves frequently updated product documentation, and accesses order information through an internal API. The solution must preserve context across multi-turn interactions, retrieve current product information, perform order-related operations, and maintain detailed audit trails showing which knowledge sources and backend tools contributed to each response. The company wants to minimize custom orchestration and infrastructure management. Which approach will best satisfy these requirements while minimizing operational effort?

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to coordinate product retrieval and order API calls. Store conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB and send workflow execution logs to Amazon CloudWatch for auditing.
options.rationale: because AWS Step Functions is primarily designed to orchestrate application workflows rather than provide purpose-built agent memory, session context, and managed tool discovery. This architecture would require the company to create separate persistence, retrieval, and orchestration mechanisms that AgentCore Memory and Gateway already provide.

options.text: Deploy the agent with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory to preserve context across multi-turn interactions. Register the order management REST API and an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base as tools in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and enable Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability to trace knowledge retrieval, tool invocations, and response processing for audit trails.

Deploy the agent on AWS Lambda and store session history in Amazon ElastiCache. Query Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases separately and invoke the order management API through Amazon API Gateway from custom application logic.
options.rationale: because this approach would simply move memory management, tool routing, and knowledge retrieval into custom application code. AgentCore Gateway already exposes REST API operations and managed Knowledge Bases as tools through a unified interface, while AgentCore Memory provides managed session-aware context.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to answer product queries and maintain conversation history in the client application. Invoke the order management API separately through AWS Lambda and store API responses in Amazon S3 for auditing.
options.rationale: because a Knowledge Base is typically focused on retrieving relevant enterprise information rather than orchestrating transactional API operations or managing the complete agent session. Keeping conversation history in the client and handling order operations separately would fragment the workflow and require additional coordination compared with AgentCore Runtime, Memory, Gateway, and Observability.

correct_text: Deploy the agent with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory to preserve context across multi-turn interactions. Register the order management REST API and an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base as tools in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and enable Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability to trace knowledge retrieval, tool invocations, and response processing for audit trails.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A healthcare network uses Amazon Bedrock to generate discharge summaries from physician notes, lab results, and imaging reports. The current prompt works well for routine cases, but complex patient records produce noticeable inconsistencies in completeness, terminology, and key clinical details. The company wants to determine which prompt changes improve summary quality across difficult cases, compare prompt versions against measurable quality targets, and retain a history of prompt changes and evaluation results for future review. Which approach will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Track prompt changes in a version-controlled repository and validate each revision against a benchmark set of complex clinical documents using measurable evaluation criteria. Automate side-by-side testing to identify quality regressions, improvements, and consistent performance patterns across prompt versions.
Refine the existing prompt based on a small sample of problematic summaries and manually review the outputs before deploying each updated version to Bedrock.
options.rationale: because a small, manually reviewed sample would simply provide limited and inconsistent evidence about prompt quality. It does not establish a repeatable benchmark, measurable acceptance criteria, or automated regression testing across prompt revisions. Amazon Bedrock evaluations are designed to use defined prompt datasets and metrics so results can be compared systematically.

options.text: Create separate prompts for simple and complex clinical documents and route each document type to the corresponding prompt based on document length and structure.
options.rationale: because this approach primarily changes how requests are routed rather than determining why one prompt performs better than another. It does not provide metric-based comparison, regression detection, or a historical record of prompt performance across the same benchmark cases.

options.text: Fine-tune a model with previously accepted clinical summaries and use the customized model for complex documents while continuing to use the current prompt for routine cases.
options.rationale: because fine-tuning is typically a more substantial model-customization step than necessary for a problem that has first been identified as prompt inconsistency. Before modifying the model itself, the company should establish a repeatable evaluation process to determine whether prompt revisions can resolve the observed quality issues and quantify the effect of those changes.

correct_text: Track prompt changes in a version-controlled repository and validate each revision against a benchmark set of complex clinical documents using measurable evaluation criteria. Automate side-by-side testing to identify quality regressions, improvements, and consistent performance patterns across prompt versions.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A global wildlife research organization is developing an automated monitoring system to track endangered species using camera trap images collected from remote conservation areas. Image data is uploaded to Amazon S3, and Amazon Rekognition performs an initial scan to identify frames that likely contain animals instead of empty backgrounds. Filtered images are then passed to a custom deep learning model, built using an Amazon SageMaker AI algorithm, to detect and count individual animals within each image accurately. The project requires distinguishing between multiple species, such as elephants, tigers, and rhinos, while also determining the exact position of each animal in the frame. Bounding boxes must be generated for every detected animal to analyze population density and movement patterns over time. The final model will be integrated into an automated analytics pipeline that updates a conservation dashboard used by field researchers and policy teams. Which modeling approach should be implemented in SageMaker AI to both identify animal species and locate each one precisely within the images?

options.text: Use a SageMaker AI algorithm for semantic segmentation to label every pixel in the image.
options.rationale: . Semantic segmentation focuses on classifying each pixel in an image, not on identifying individual objects or assigning distinct bounding boxes. It would only tell which pixels belong to an animal, but not distinguish between multiple animals of the same class.

options.text: Train a SageMaker AI algorithm for image classification to categorize the dominant species in an image without detecting specific locations.
options.rationale: . Image classification simply predicts a single label (or set of labels) for an entire image and does not provide spatial information. It would only indicate which species are present overall, rather than identifying where each animal appears. This method is typically used for tasks where object localization is irrelevant, such as determining general content or scene type.

options.text: Deploy a custom pose estimation model in SageMaker AI to identify animal skeletal keypoints and postures rather than detecting full animal objects or their locations.
options.rationale: . Pose estimation models are primarily designed to analyze body posture or joint positions of detected subjects. While useful for understanding movement patterns, pose estimation does not inherently perform full object detection or species classification. It would only identify keypoints, such as limbs or facial landmarks, not the bounding boxes or labels needed for population tracking and species identification.

options.text: Use a SageMaker AI object detection algorithm to accurately identify and localize multiple animal species by generating bounding boxes and associated class labels.

correct_text: Use a SageMaker AI object detection algorithm to accurately identify and localize multiple animal species by generating bounding boxes and associated class labels.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A digital publishing company uses Amazon Bedrock to generate articles, advertisements, and social media content. Several development teams maintain hundreds of reusable prompt templates and deploy approved templates to applications in multiple AWS Regions. The company requires a centralized governance process that preserves prompt versions, standardizes prompt variables and inference configurations, and prevents unapproved templates from reaching production. Reviewers must receive notifications when a prompt is awaiting approval. The governance team must also be able to determine which identity created, modified, approved, or deployed each prompt. Which architecture should the company implement to satisfy these governance objectives?

options.text: Build the approval process with AWS Step Functions. Store prompt documents in Amazon S3 and apply object tags to track versions. Configure Amazon EventBridge to deliver notifications when reviews are pending.
options.rationale: because AWS Step Functions can just implement a workflow that pauses for human approval, and Amazon EventBridge can route workflow events to notification targets. However, this approach requires a custom approval implementation and stores prompts as ordinary Amazon S3 objects rather than as managed Amazon Bedrock prompts.

options.text: Store prompt templates in Amazon S3 with S3 Versioning enabled. Configure AWS CodePipeline manual approval actions and Amazon SNS notifications before deployment. Use AWS CloudTrail to record S3 object activity and apply IAM policies to control access to the prompt files.
options.rationale: because S3 Versioning can preserve multiple versions of a prompt document, and CodePipeline can provide the required approval checkpoint and notifications. However, the prompts remain ordinary files instead of Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management resources.

options.text: Manage parameterized prompt templates with variables and create numbered versions using Bedrock Prompt Management. Add an AWS CodePipeline manual approval action with Amazon SNS notifications before deployment. Use IAM to separate responsibilities and AWS CloudTrail to record API activity.

Deploy the applications with Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Use AgentCore Identity and IAM for reviewer access, AgentCore Observability for prompt tracing, and Amazon EventBridge for review notifications. Store prompt revisions in AgentCore Memory.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is designed only for deploying, securing, operating, and observing AI agents and tools. AgentCore Memory retains contextual information from agent interactions rather than version-controlled prompt templates. These capabilities do not replace Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management for creating reusable prompts, defining variables and inference configurations, and preserving numbered prompt versions.

correct_text: Manage parameterized prompt templates with variables and create numbered versions using Bedrock Prompt Management. Add an AWS CodePipeline manual approval action with Amazon SNS notifications before deployment. Use IAM to separate responsibilities and AWS CloudTrail to record API activity.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A regulated financial services organization is rolling out AI governance policies to control how internal applications interact with foundation models (FMs). The governance team mandates that all FM interactions must be protected by guardrails to ensure responsible AI usage and prevent policy violations. The company uses Amazon Bedrock guardrails and allows application teams to directly call Bedrock APIs. Security architects must design a solution that: Enforces guardrail usage for all FM interactions Applies to both InvokeModel and Converse API calls Prevents any request from bypassing guardrails Which solution enforces these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Apply AWS IAM access controls to InvokeModel and Converse API actions that require both the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier and bedrock:PromptRouterArn condition keys, and mandate that all requests pass through a prompt router to attach and validate guardrails before invoking Bedrock foundation models.
options.rationale: because forcing all traffic through a prompt router introduces unnecessary architectural complexity and operational overhead. Guardrail enforcement does not require a routing layer when IAM can already mandate the presence of a guardrail identifier directly on the Bedrock API calls.

options.text: Deploy an API Gateway and AWS Lambda proxy that injects guardrails into all InvokeModel and Converse API requests before forwarding them to Bedrock.
options.rationale: because it typically requires building and maintaining custom infrastructure (API Gateway and Lambda). This adds significant operational overhead compared to IAM-based enforcement, and still leaves room for misconfiguration or bypass if applications call Bedrock directly.

options.text: Store the guardrail identifier in AWS Secrets Manager and require applications to retrieve it before calling InvokeModel or Converse API.
options.rationale: because simply storing the guardrail ID does not enforce its usage. Applications could bypass retrieval or call Bedrock directly without attaching the guardrail, so this does not guarantee compliance.

options.text: Enforce AWS IAM policies on InvokeModel and Converse API actions that require the presence of a bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier, ensuring that all Bedrock foundation model requests include an attached guardrail.

correct_text: Enforce AWS IAM policies on InvokeModel and Converse API actions that require the presence of a bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier, ensuring that all Bedrock foundation model requests include an attached guardrail.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A financial services company uses Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks for data exploration and SageMaker Autopilot to train ML models on customer data stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The dataset contains sensitive financial information, and compliance policies require that all data traffic remain within the AWS private network. During an audit, the security team discovers that SageMaker Studio is accessing S3 over the public internet. The AI developer must reconfigure the environment to ensure that all data transfers between SageMaker and S3 occur securely within AWS’s internal network while maintaining full functionality for Studio notebooks and Autopilot jobs. Which configuration should the developer implement to meet this requirement?

options.text: Configure SageMaker Studio notebooks to run within a VPC and create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 to ensure all traffic between SageMaker and S3 stays within the AWS private network.
Enable SageMaker Studio internet access and use AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for encrypting data in transit.
options.rationale: . This option is primarily focused on securing data in transit via encryption, but it does not prevent traffic from traversing the public internet. While encryption ensures confidentiality, it does not meet the compliance requirement of keeping all data access entirely within AWS’s private network. This approach would still expose S3 requests to the internet, making it simply insufficient for the organization’s security policy.

options.text: Create a public S3 Access Point and restrict it to the SageMaker IAM role for data retrieval during training.
options.rationale: . Using a public S3 Access Point may only control which IAM role can access the data, but it does not restrict network traffic to remain within the AWS private environment. Requests would still flow over the public internet, which typically violates compliance requirements for sensitive financial data.

options.text: Enable AWS PrivateLink for S3 and configure SageMaker Studio to route traffic through the interface endpoint for private connectivity.
options.rationale: . While AWS PrivateLink can provide private connectivity for certain AWS services, S3 primarily supports VPC Gateway Endpoints for high-throughput, cost-effective, and private access. Using PrivateLink would primarily increase complexity and is not recommended as the approach for accessing S3 from SageMaker within a VPC. This makes it a less practical solution compared to a Gateway Endpoint.

correct_text: Configure SageMaker Studio notebooks to run within a VPC and create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 to ensure all traffic between SageMaker and S3 stays within the AWS private network.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A large online gaming company is developing a generative AI assistant that provides real-time coaching and support during live multiplayer sessions. The assistant must generate responses with very low latency during sudden traffic surges caused by tournaments and major game releases. The company wants predictable model capacity during sustained peak demand while staying within a fixed monthly compute budget. The overall architecture must also preserve auto-scaling capabilities so application components can expand or contract as traffic changes without manual intervention. Which approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use standard on-demand inference in Amazon Bedrock and request higher service quotas to handle peak traffic. Configure auto-scaling policies for the supporting application resources and monitor usage to keep monthly spending within the compute budget.
options.rationale: because on-demand inference typically provides capacity without reserving dedicated model throughput. Increasing quotas can allow more requests, but it does not provide the same predictable dedicated capacity and fixed Provisioned Throughput cost structure needed for sustained peak demand.

options.text: Select an Amazon Bedrock model that provides low-latency inference for real-time workloads and allocate Provisioned Throughput for predictable model capacity. Configure auto-scaling policies for the supporting application resources to adjust automatically as demand changes.

Utilize latency-optimized inference in Amazon Bedrock with cross-Region inference to distribute requests across supported Regions. Rely on on-demand capacity during traffic spikes and configure auto-scaling for the application tier.
options.rationale: because this approach would simply optimize responsiveness and distribute requests across Regions while still relying on on-demand inference capacity. In addition, AWS states that inference profiles used for cross-Region inference currently do not support Provisioned Throughput, so this design does not provide the dedicated capacity required by the scenario.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock batch inference to process incoming requests in large groups during peak periods. Scale the supporting application resources automatically and schedule processing windows to control monthly compute costs.
options.rationale: because batch inference is primarily designed for asynchronous processing of multiple prompts. Results are written to Amazon S3 after the batch job completes, which does not meet the requirement for interactive, low-latency coaching during live multiplayer sessions. AWS also notes that batch inference is not supported for provisioned models.

correct_text: Select an Amazon Bedrock model that provides low-latency inference for real-time workloads and allocate Provisioned Throughput for predictable model capacity. Configure auto-scaling policies for the supporting application resources to adjust automatically as demand changes.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A financial services organization is developing a generative AI chatbot using Amazon Bedrock to answer confidential customer questions. The solution must implement layered protection mechanisms to prevent advanced prompt injection attacks targeting the model. Security engineers also require detailed audit records whenever safety rules intervene, such as when model input or output is blocked or modified. In addition, the architecture must support multi-Region resilience so the AI assistant continues functioning if a Region becomes unavailable. Which architecture satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Enable Bedrock guardrails with strict content filters and attach AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) to the API endpoint to inspect incoming requests. Record activity using AWS CloudTrail API event logs.
options.rationale: because these services operate primarily at the network/API layer rather than the generative model safety layer. WAF can filter HTTP requests and block malicious patterns, but prompt injection occurs inside the model prompt context, which WAF cannot reliably analyze. Additionally, CloudTrail records API activity, not guardrail intervention events, meaning detailed AI safety actions would not be captured.

options.text: Implement Amazon Comprehend custom classifiers to detect prompt injection attacks before requests reach the model. Use Amazon API Gateway request validation and export logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
options.rationale: because this design just introduces custom NLP classifiers to detect prompt injection attempts. Prompt injection techniques often exploit model-specific prompt behavior, which traditional NLP classifiers may fail to detect reliably. Although CloudWatch Logs could capture events, this option still lacks Bedrock-native guardrail enforcement and cross-Region guardrail capabilities.

options.text: Configure Bedrock guardrails with strict word filters and enable multi-Region deployment of the application with log auditing stored in AWS CloudTrail.
options.rationale: because it relies mainly on word filters and application multi-Region deployment. Simple keyword or word filters are insufficient to detect sophisticated prompt injection patterns, which often rely on contextual manipulation rather than specific keywords. Furthermore, CloudTrail logs API-level operations, not detailed guardrail intervention events such as blocked prompts or filtered responses.

options.text: Configure Bedrock guardrails with content filters set to a high threshold to mitigate prompt injection attacks. Apply a guardrail profile to enable cross-Region guardrail inference. Send detailed guardrail intervention logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and create custom metrics for monitoring.

correct_text: Configure Bedrock guardrails with content filters set to a high threshold to mitigate prompt injection attacks. Apply a guardrail profile to enable cross-Region guardrail inference. Send detailed guardrail intervention logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and create custom metrics for monitoring.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A multinational publishing company is developing an internal AI-powered assistant to help employees retrieve, summarize, and analyze research documents. The company’s data-science team already relies on Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth to label training data and improve metadata accuracy. The next development phase involves integrating AI agents in Amazon Bedrock that can autonomously answer questions, summarize lengthy documents, and recommend related content. To achieve this, the team requires a mechanism that can represent both user queries and document content as semantic embeddings that capture contextual relationships between concepts and terms. The solution must be fully managed, scalable, and easily integrated with existing AWS services to support downstream retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows. Given the large volume of documents, the team also needs to optimize performance by implementing appropriate data distribution and query-handling strategies. Which approach best satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Implement Amazon Kendra to index research documents, support natural-language queries, and enable AI agents to retrieve relevant results via the service's managed semantic search and ranking capabilities.
options.rationale: because Amazon Kendra is primarily designed as an enterprise search service that indexes and retrieves documents from data sources using natural-language queries. While it supports semantic search through ranking and FAQ matching, it does not generate or manage vector embeddings required for semantic retrieval or integration with AI agents in Amazon Bedrock for context-aware reasoning.

options.text: Deploy SageMaker JumpStart to fine-tune and host a pre-trained language model for summarization and text generation, integrating it with AI agents for enhanced content discovery workflows.
options.rationale: because Amazon SageMaker JumpStart only provides pre-trained models for quick deployment and fine-tuning within SageMaker. Although it accelerates model customization and hosting, it does not handle embedding generation or perform vector similarity searches necessary for retrieval-augmented generation workflows in Amazon Bedrock.

options.text: Leverage Amazon Titan Text Embeddings in Bedrock to convert text into semantic vectors and store them in Amazon OpenSearch Service for context-aware retrieval and reasoning by AI agents. Implement OpenSearch sharding strategies to distribute the vector index across multiple nodes for optimal query performance and horizontal scalability.

Configure SageMaker Data Wrangler to preprocess textual data, extract engineered features through clustering, and allow AI agents to analyze document similarity within structured datasets and grouped content.
options.rationale: because Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler is typically used for preparing, cleaning, and transforming data before model training. It supports visualization and feature engineering but does not create or store text embeddings, nor does it enable vector-based search or semantic reasoning capabilities for generative AI agents.

correct_text: Leverage Amazon Titan Text Embeddings in Bedrock to convert text into semantic vectors and store them in Amazon OpenSearch Service for context-aware retrieval and reasoning by AI agents. Implement OpenSearch sharding strategies to distribute the vector index across multiple nodes for optimal query performance and horizontal scalability.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A startup is training an autonomous vehicle detection model using Amazon SageMaker AI with labeled image data stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The dataset is annotated using SageMaker Ground Truth, which contains thousands of high-resolution images. During model training, the team observes slow startup times and low GPU utilization because the training job downloads data sequentially from S3. The company wants to keep the S3 bucket as the primary data repository, but improve data access performance and training throughput for SageMaker AI without duplicating data or significantly altering the training script. The team reviewed AWS Cost Explorer and observed rising GPU costs due to idle compute time. Which solution should be implemented to optimize SageMaker AI training performance while maintaining the existing S3-based workflow?

options.text: Use Amazon EFS to store the training data and mount it directly to the SageMaker AI training container for faster sequential reads.
options.rationale: . Amazon EFS is designed for general-purpose, shared file storage rather than high-performance, parallel data access. It is typically suited for workloads that require low to moderate throughput and concurrent file access across multiple instances, such as web applications or content management systems. While SageMaker can mount EFS, it does not deliver the same throughput and IOPS performance as Amazon FSx for Lustre for large-scale ML training. Using EFS would only marginally improve performance and would not address the high-volume parallel read requirements of GPU-accelerated training jobs.

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system and connect it to the existing S3 bucket. Update the SageMaker AI training job to access the dataset directly from the FSx mount.
Copy the dataset from S3 to local Amazon EBS volumes before each SageMaker AI training run to eliminate data transfer delays.
options.rationale: . Copying data before every training run increases setup time, consumes additional storage, and leads to cost inefficiencies for large datasets. It also introduces potential versioning inconsistencies if the data in S3 changes. While local EBS storage provides low-latency access during training, it only benefits a single training job at a time. It must be reinitialized for each new run, which contradicts the goal of maintaining a scalable, automated pipeline.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to reduce latency when downloading data during each training job.
options.rationale: . S3 Transfer Acceleration enhances upload and download speeds for long-distance transfers over the public internet, primarily benefiting cross-region or geographically distributed clients. In this case, SageMaker and S3 are operating within the same AWS Region, where latency is already minimal. Therefore, enabling Transfer Acceleration would not meaningfully reduce intra-region data access time or address the sequential download bottleneck. The issue lies in throughput and parallel access, not network latency, making this configuration ineffective for the described scenario.

correct_text: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system and connect it to the existing S3 bucket. Update the SageMaker AI training job to access the dataset directly from the FSx mount.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A multinational financial services company is developing an AI-powered assistant to assist risk analysts in reviewing and monitoring client portfolios. The system uses Amazon Bedrock to run a foundation model for natural-language reasoning and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to fine-tune embeddings on historical portfolio data, regulatory filings, and market research. Analysts require access to multiple data sources, including live stock and bond prices streamed through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, as well as operational alerts from Amazon CloudWatch. The architecture must allow the foundation model to query these sources dynamically, securely, and consistently, without embedding API calls, SQL queries, or credentials directly into the prompts. Which design approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Implement Lambda functions that encapsulate the API logic for Kinesis, CloudWatch, and SageMaker embeddings. Have the foundation model generate the invocation syntax in its prompts to call each function.
options.rationale: because it relies on the model to correctly generate backend calls, which can lead to inconsistent or failed queries. It also does not centralize access control, logging, or validation, making the solution less secure and harder to maintain compared to using a standardized service interface.

options.text: Deploy a single intermediate service that securely exposes Kinesis, CloudWatch, and SageMaker embeddings as callable tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing Bedrock to query each source dynamically.
Use SageMaker JumpStart embeddings alone and rely on the foundation model’s general financial knowledge.
options.rationale: . Relying solely on embeddings and the model’s general knowledge is insufficient for this workload. Embeddings can enrich contextual understanding, but they cannot typically provide real-time stock prices, operational alerts, or historical Redshift transactions. This option only addresses semantic search and ignores the need for dynamic, secure querying of live enterprise data, making it misaligned with the system’s core requirements.

options.text: Deploy separate microservices for each data source and rely on prompt-based routing in Bedrock to dynamically select which service to query.
options.rationale: . While microservices are technically feasible, this approach is inefficient because it introduces unnecessary operational overhead. Having multiple independent services forces the model to simply infer which microservice to call, which is error-prone and difficult to secure. Prompt-based routing is primarily unreliable, as the model may misinterpret instructions or hallucinate service names. A unified MCP-based tool layer provides predictable, permission-controlled access, while this option does not.

correct_text: Deploy a single intermediate service that securely exposes Kinesis, CloudWatch, and SageMaker embeddings as callable tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing Bedrock to query each source dynamically.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A social media platform is developing an ML model to moderate user-generated content. The platform stores large volumes of textual and document data in Amazon S3. It uses Amazon Textract to extract text from uploaded PDFs or images, and Amazon SageMaker AI to train custom language models that classify comments based on sentiment, context, and topic relevance. The moderation team aims to enhance safety by detecting toxic or harmful language in real-time, including hate speech, harassment, and explicit threats. The solution must integrate seamlessly with the existing SageMaker AI inference pipeline, handle high throughput, and provide confidence scores for each classification, allowing content flagged as toxic to be reviewed or blocked automatically. Which of the solutions provides a managed solution for detecting toxicity in text to support this ML pipeline with safety classifiers?

options.text: Utilize Amazon Comprehend sentiment analysis to detect negative comments and block content automatically.
options.rationale: because sentiment analysis only identifies the overall tone of text as positive, negative, or neutral. It does not specifically detect abusive or toxic language, so relying on it would typically miss harmful content or misclassify non-toxic negative comments as toxic.

options.text: Use Amazon Translate to convert text into another language before moderation to reduce offensive content.
options.rationale: . Amazon Translation does not inherently detect toxicity. It simply converts text from one language to another, which would only change the language but not address abusive or harmful content. Moderation would remain ineffective if the goal is to identify toxic text.

options.text: Utilize Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection to identify abusive or harmful language in text.
Use Amazon Bedrock to fine-tune a foundation model for general language understanding.
options.rationale: . While Bedrock can be used to fine-tune foundation models, it does not automatically detect toxic language. Fine-tuning for general language understanding only provides broader NLP capabilities, and toxicity detection would require additional custom development, which is typically more complex and time-consuming than using a managed service like Comprehend.

correct_text: Utilize Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection to identify abusive or harmful language in text.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A global e-commerce company has deployed a customer service chatbot powered by Amazon Bedrock for real-time query processing. The application uses server-sent events to stream generated responses to client interfaces as they become available. The chatbot uses Amazon SageMaker AI for model training and inference and utilizes a cross-region inference profile to optimize throughput. The company must ensure that input prompts and output results are transmitted securely across regions, with data remaining within the designated geography (the US) to meet compliance requirements. Additionally, the system must stay scalable and responsive during peak traffic bursts, leveraging AWS services to handle traffic fluctuations and ensure consistent performance during high-demand periods. Which approach should satisfy the requirement?

options.text: Use Bedrock with a global cross-region inference profile, allowing the system to route requests to the best-performing AWS Regions worldwide, increasing throughput and enhancing model performance. Use Amazon Kendra for query-based search to enhance user experience and ensure relevant responses.
options.rationale: because it routes requests outside the US Regions. This simply violates the requirement to keep data within the US for compliance reasons, as the scenario specifies that data should remain within the US geography. A global cross-region profile would route requests to any commercial AWS Region globally, which contradicts the compliance requirement of geography-bound data storage and processing.

options.text: Implement a cross-region inference profile tied to the US geography and route requests to destination Regions within the US. Utilize SageMaker AI to handle model inference at peak times by enabling Provisioned Throughput, ensuring consistent performance during traffic bursts.
options.rationale: because Provisioned Throughput is not supported with cross-region inference profiles in Amazon Bedrock. While SageMaker AI is an excellent tool for handling model inference, it doesn’t address the need for Bedrock’s cross-region inference mechanism, which is primarily designed to handle traffic bursts across multiple Regions within a defined geography. Moreover, SageMaker AI does not provide the same level of orchestration for managing cross-Region inference traffic.

options.text: Configure Bedrock with a cross-region inference profile tied to the US geography and use Amazon Comprehend to analyze and categorize customer queries before routing the inference request, ensuring that only relevant queries are processed for improved throughput.
options.rationale: because Amazon Comprehend is a text analysis service and does not directly relate to traffic management or routing for cross-Region inference in Amazon Bedrock. Comprehend can analyze text for sentiment, entities, and other aspects, but it is not designed to handle cross-region traffic or routing. The primary focus in this scenario is on routing inference requests to the optimal Regions for better throughput and performance, not on text analysis or query categorization.

options.text: Use Bedrock with a cross-region inference profile tied to the US geography, ensuring that requests from US Regions are routed to the optimal destination Regions within the US, while ensuring that input prompts and output results remain encrypted during transmission across Regions. Additionally, use AWS Step Functions to manage traffic bursts and ensure that service quotas are not exceeded.

correct_text: Use Bedrock with a cross-region inference profile tied to the US geography, ensuring that requests from US Regions are routed to the optimal destination Regions within the US, while ensuring that input prompts and output results remain encrypted during transmission across Regions. Additionally, use AWS Step Functions to manage traffic bursts and ensure that service quotas are not exceeded.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A large retail company is looking to leverage Amazon SageMaker AI notebooks and Amazon Comprehend to process and analyze customer feedback data. The company uses Amazon S3 buckets to store large datasets of customer reviews, and the data needs to be accessed securely for machine learning analysis. Given the sensitivity of the data, the company mandates that all resources must remain within a secure Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Additionally, all communication must occur over the AWS network. Which solution will satisfy the given requirements?

options.text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet with a route to an internet gateway and ensure that all data requests to S3 are routed through an external proxy.
options.rationale: because routing through an internet gateway and external proxy exposes traffic to the public internet, violating the requirement that all communication must occur over a private AWS network.

options.text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet within a VPC and use a VPC Peering connection with another VPC where S3 is accessible.
options.rationale: because VPC peering does not typically provide private access to AWS services like S3. Accessing S3 through a peered VPC still requires public endpoints unless VPC endpoints are configured, which this option does not guarantee.

options.text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet within a VPC and ensure that the VPC has private endpoints for both SageMaker AI and S3.
Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet, use a NAT gateway to provide outbound internet access for S3, and restrict access to only specific S3 buckets.
options.rationale: because using a NAT gateway primarily involves public internet routing, which contradicts the mandate for a private AWS network. Even with bucket restrictions, the traffic path does not meet the security requirements.

correct_text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet within a VPC and ensure that the VPC has private endpoints for both SageMaker AI and S3.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A company is developing an incident analysis assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs) to provide real-time AI assistance to security analysts investigating alerts and suspicious activity. The assistant generates remediation guidance and investigation summaries, but complex requests can take several seconds to complete. The analysts need AI-generated responses to appear incrementally as generated so it can begin reviewing recommendations immediately. The application must handle thousands of concurrent analyst sessions while maintaining minimal latency and avoiding long waits for complete model responses. Which architecture will best satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda integration. Have the Lambda function invoke the Bedrock InvokeModel API and return the complete response to the client after generation finishes.
options.rationale: because IInvokeModel typically follows a request-response pattern in which the application receives the model output after inference processing. It does not provide the incremental response chunks required for analysts to begin reading the answer while it is still being generated. The streaming API is the appropriate Bedrock operation for this requirement.

options.text: Set up an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API integrated with AWS Lambda. Have the Lambda function invoke the Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream API and send each partial model response to connected clients through the WebSocket API.

Set up an AWS Lambda function to invoke the Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream API and store partial responses in Amazon DynamoDB. Have client applications poll the table through Amazon API Gateway to retrieve newly generated response segments.
options.rationale: because storing chunks and polling for them would simply introduce additional database operations and repeated client requests. API Gateway WebSocket APIs allow backend services to push messages directly to connected clients, eliminating the polling mechanism and better supporting the minimal-latency requirement.

options.text: Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda integration that invokes the Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream API. Buffer the streamed output in the Lambda function and return the completed response in a single HTTP response.
options.rationale: because buffering the output only uses the streaming API internally. The end user would still wait until the complete response had been assembled before receiving any content, defeating the requirement to display AI-generated responses incrementally. InvokeModelWithResponseStream is designed to make response chunks available without waiting for the entire result.

correct_text: Set up an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API integrated with AWS Lambda. Have the Lambda function invoke the Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream API and send each partial model response to connected clients through the WebSocket API.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A global insurance provider processes tens of thousands of scanned policy agreements, claim submissions, and regulatory filings every day. To extract textual content from a variety of unstructured documents, the company utilizes Amazon Textract. After the data is extracted, Amazon Comprehend analyzes it to identify and classify key entities such as policy identifiers and coverage terms, while Comprehend Medical focuses on identifying medical conditions and related terminology. However, challenges arise due to inconsistent formatting, variations in terminology, abbreviations, and inaccuracies in optical character recognition (OCR), which can impede accurate entity recognition and large-scale data extraction. Certain documents fail automated validation workflows, necessitating intervention by a team of human analysts. This manual review process creates operational bottlenecks, prolongs turnaround times, and increases processing costs. The organization seeks to streamline document processing. The new workflow should reduce reliance on manual review while maintaining high precision and recall in extracted data, ensuring that downstream systems can reliably consume the information for decision-making and compliance purposes. What is the most effective way to improve automated insurance application processing?

options.text: Deploy an Amazon Bedrock’s Claude model to re-analyze low-confidence extracted insurance application text to refine validation predictions, then route the outputs for manual review.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock is primarily designed for accessing and deploying foundation models for text generation, summarization, and conversational AI. It does not provide built-in capabilities for human-in-the-loop validation or confidence-based review workflows. Bedrock does not integrate directly with Amazon Textract to route low-confidence predictions for verification, making it unsuitable for document validation scenarios.

options.text: Use Textract to flag words with low confidence and send them to Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for manual inspection before validation.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Ground Truth is only intended for building and managing labeled datasets for training or retraining machine learning models. It is not meant for real-time document validation or human review of production workloads. Ground Truth lacks native integration with Textract for automated verification workflows, so it cannot effectively address the need for continuous document accuracy checks.

options.text: Set up Textract to forward low-confidence predictions to Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) for verification prior to executing validation workflows.
Further automate insurance application validation by sending extracted text to an Amazon Titan foundation model to predict errors without human review.
options.rationale: because Titan models are typically used for generative AI tasks such as content creation or text embedding, not for deterministic validation of OCR accuracy. Also, using a foundation model without human verification would simply increase the likelihood of data errors or misinterpretations, as these models are not designed to replace confidence scoring or human review in compliance-driven document processing.

correct_text: Set up Textract to forward low-confidence predictions to Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) for verification prior to executing validation workflows.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A retail company is developing an AI-based recommendation system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The system will leverage a large language model (LLM) fine-tuned in Amazon SageMaker AI to generate personalized product recommendations based on user browsing behavior. The solution must ensure secure, real-time inference within the Bedrock environment, while also maintaining scalability and operational efficiency. Additionally, the company wants to monitor the inference latency and model performance metrics in real-time using Amazon CloudWatch. The architecture team has also evaluated AWS Agent Squad for potential multi-agent orchestration capabilities in future recommendation workflows. Which solution ensures secure and scalable inference while minimizing operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy the fine-tuned LLM to SageMaker AI, configure an AWS Lambda function to invoke SageMaker endpoints, and monitor performance using CloudWatch metrics.
options.rationale: . This approach simply introduces unnecessary complexity and operational overhead. While deploying the model to SageMaker AI is feasible, integrating it with a Lambda function for invoking endpoints adds a layer that requires manual management and scaling. This setup deviates from the streamlined, serverless experience that Amazon Bedrock’s Custom Model Import offers, which is designed to reduce infrastructure management efforts. Furthermore, relying on Lambda functions can lead to increased latency and potential cold start issues, which are less optimal compared to the on-demand, low-latency inference provided by Bedrock.

options.text: Import the fine-tuned model directly into Bedrock using the Custom Model Import, assign an AgentCore-managed execution role, and set up CloudWatch for real-time monitoring of model metrics.
Host the LLM on an Amazon EC2 instance, connect it to Bedrock AgentCore via a REST API, and use CloudWatch Logs to monitor the API calls.
options.rationale: because hosting the model on an EC2 instance typically requires manual provisioning, scaling, and maintenance, which increases operational complexity. Integrating this setup with Bedrock AgentCore via a REST API introduces additional points of failure and potential latency issues. This approach also lacks the seamless integration with Bedrock’s native features like Knowledge Bases, Guardrails, and Agents, which are readily accessible when using the Custom Model Import API. Moreover, managing EC2 instances for model hosting does not align with the serverless paradigm that Amazon Bedrock promotes, leading to higher costs and maintenance efforts.

options.text: Store the model in Amazon S3, configure Bedrock AgentCore to load the model during runtime, and use CloudWatch to monitor API performance.
options.rationale: . While storing the model in Amazon S3 is a valid storage solution, configuring Bedrock AgentCore to load the model during runtime can introduce performance bottlenecks. Loading models dynamically at inference time may lead to increased latency, especially for large models, and is generally less efficient than having the model preloaded and ready for inference. This method also bypasses the benefits of the Custom Model Import API, which ensures that models are optimized for performance and seamlessly integrated with Bedrock’s infrastructure.

correct_text: Import the fine-tuned model directly into Bedrock using the Custom Model Import, assign an AgentCore-managed execution role, and set up CloudWatch for real-time monitoring of model metrics.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A global retail analytics organization relies on Amazon SageMaker AI for training complex demand forecasting models while Amazon Comprehend processes multilingual customer feedback across several continents. During a major international sales period, the generative AI assistant that the company operates using Amazon Bedrock experiences a sudden and unpredictable rise in inference requests originating from users in Europe and the Asia Pacific region. The engineering teams must ensure that the assistant continues to provide low-latency responses for all global users while meeting strict data residency requirements with the least operational overhead. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Use SageMaker AI inference endpoints deployed in multiple regions and direct incoming traffic to the closest region through a latency-based routing policy in Amazon Route 53.
options.rationale: because this requires managing separate inference endpoints, increasing operational overhead, and also does not address the Bedrock-based generative assistant workload directly.

options.text: Use Comprehend real-time processing in a central region and copy customer interaction data to nearby regions ahead of anticipated demand.
options.rationale: because the problem is related to scaling Bedrock inference, not Comprehend text-processing. This option does not primarily address low-latency generative AI inference nor data-residency requirements for Bedrock.

options.text: Use the Bedrock cross-region inference profile so that inference calls from one region are automatically routed to another region that has available compute capacity.
Deploy the chosen foundation model in each region across Europe and the Asia Pacific region through Bedrock and manage traffic distribution with a custom client-side routing mechanism.
options.rationale: because it typically requires building and maintaining a custom client-side routing solution, which introduces significant operational overhead and complexity.

correct_text: Use the Bedrock cross-region inference profile so that inference calls from one region are automatically routed to another region that has available compute capacity.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A global e-commerce company uses Amazon Bedrock with the Amazon Titan foundation model (FM) to power a multilingual customer support chatbot. In addition to Titan FM, the company also uses Amazon Comprehend to perform entity recognition and sentiment analysis on incoming customer messages. However, the support chatbot often provides generic answers because it lacks access to the company’s proprietary order management and product documentation data stored in Amazon S3 and an internal database. The AI developer wants to enhance the chatbot’s responses with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) so that Titan FM can generate more accurate and contextually relevant replies based on real-time, private company data, without retraining the model. Which of the following options will satisfy this requirement?

options.text: Fine-tune the Amazon Titan foundation model with the company’s support data using Amazon SageMaker AI.
options.rationale: because it involves retraining the model, which contradicts the requirement to enhance responses without retraining. Fine-tuning is resource-intensive and not necessary when RAG can achieve contextual relevance by dynamically retrieving data.

options.text: Increase the temperature parameter for the Amazon Titan model to improve contextual understanding.
options.rationale: because temperature primarily controls the randomness or creativity of the model’s output, not its ability to access or understand proprietary data. Raising the temperature might make responses more varied, but it won’t improve factual accuracy or relevance to internal company data.

options.text: Set up a Bedrock knowledge base and integrate it with the company’s private data sources.
Use the Comprehend custom classification to provide the model with retrieval capabilities.
options.rationale: because Amazon Comprehend is typically designed for NLP tasks like entity recognition and sentiment analysis, not for retrieval or grounding model outputs in external data. It cannot connect Titan FM to private databases or documents for RAG.

correct_text: Set up a Bedrock knowledge base and integrate it with the company’s private data sources.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A digital media company operates a web platform where customers upload high-resolution product and marketing images that require automated text generation for accessibility and search optimization. Each uploaded image can reach up to 60 MB in size, and the platform experiences unpredictable spikes in traffic during global promotional campaigns. All uploaded images are securely stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, which acts as the central repository for incoming media files. The company uses Amazon Rekognition to analyze images, detecting objects, scenes, and other visual features that form the foundation of metadata. The extracted information is passed to Amazon Bedrock, which uses a foundation model to generate detailed natural language captions describing the image content accurately and contextually. The ML workflow automatically starts processing when new images are uploaded to the S3 bucket. The GenAI developer must design a solution that scales automatically to handle fluctuating workloads, maintains high availability during traffic spikes, and operates with minimal infrastructure management overhead. Which solution fulfills these requirements with minimal infrastructure management and operational effort?

options.text: Build a containerized processing pipeline using Amazon ECS on Fargate that runs on a schedule to handle uploaded images and insert processed data into Amazon Aurora.
options.rationale: because ECS scheduled tasks are primarily designed for running periodic jobs based on a fixed schedule rather than responding to event-driven triggers such as new S3 uploads. While ECS Fargate removes the need to manage servers, it still requires manual configuration for scheduling, monitoring, and scaling. This setup would not provide the dynamic responsiveness and automated scaling required to handle unpredictable spikes in image upload volume.

options.text: Deploy an Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint with a scaling policy that automatically adjusts capacity and processes inference requests for each image in the S3 bucket.
Launch an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to host an inference application that monitors the primary S3 bucket for new image uploads and stores processed results in a separate S3 bucket.
options.rationale: because EC2-based solutions typically require ongoing infrastructure management, including instance patching, scaling configurations, and monitoring. Even though Auto Scaling provides elasticity, this approach adds operational complexity and lacks the built-in queuing and asynchronous processing capabilities of managed inference services. The result is higher administrative overhead and less efficient scaling compared to a fully managed solution like SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.

options.text: Use Amazon SQS to queue image-processing tasks and trigger AWS Lambda functions that run Rekognition and Bedrock processing for each uploaded image.
options.rationale: because Lambda is just not designed for large, resource-intensive ML workflows. Lambda has strict limits on payload size, memory, and execution time, making it unsuitable for handling high-resolution images up to 60 MB or for running long-running inference jobs. During traffic spikes, Lambda would struggle to scale efficiently for this type of workload, leading to failures or timeouts. The company needs a solution specifically designed for scalable asynchronous ML inference, which Lambda cannot provide.
